prompt: What did Max Planck propose in 1900 to explain blackbody radiation?

choices.text: Energy can be gained or lost only in whole-number multiples of a smallest unit, hν
Light can carry any amount of energy, continuously
choices.why: That is the classical view that failed. Planck proposed that energy comes in quanta of size hν.

choices.text: Electrons travel around the nucleus in circular orbits
choices.why: That is Bohr's model of 1913. Planck's idea was that energy is quantized in units of hν.

choices.text: Every particle has a wavelength λ = h/p
choices.why: That is de Broglie's idea of 1924. Planck proposed that energy is quantized.

explanation: Planck explained the blackbody spectrum by proposing that energy is quantized: the oscillators in the walls of the oven can gain or lose energy only in chunks, or quanta, of size hν.

prompt: In Planck's equation E = hν, what happens to the energy of one quantum as the frequency increases?

choices.text: It increases
It decreases
choices.why: E = hν, and h is a positive constant, so E goes up when ν goes up.

choices.text: It stays the same
choices.why: The energy of a quantum depends on its frequency: E = hν.

choices.text: It becomes zero
choices.why: A quantum always has energy hν, which grows with frequency.

explanation: E = hν: the energy of a quantum is proportional to its frequency, so higher-frequency radiation comes in larger quanta.

prompt: Use E = hν with h = 6.626 × 10^−34 J·s. What is the energy, in joules, of one quantum of radiation with a frequency of 1.00 × 10^15 Hz? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e-19.)
Which everyday picture does the section use for quantized energy?

choices.text: Climbing a staircase, where you can stand only on certain steps
Rolling a ball down a smooth ramp
choices.why: On a smooth ramp the height can take any value. That is continuous, the opposite of quantized.

choices.text: Water flowing steadily from a tap
choices.why: A steady flow can take any value. Quantized means only certain separate values are allowed.

choices.text: A car speeding up smoothly
choices.why: Smoothly changing speed is continuous. Quantization means jumps between allowed values.

explanation: The section compares quantization to going up and down a hill on stair steps rather than a continuous slope: your potential energy can take only certain values. It also mentions money in whole pennies and the fixed notes of a piano.

prompt: What are the units of Planck's constant, h?

choices.text: J·s
J/s
choices.why: J/s is a watt, a unit of power. Since E = hν and ν is in s^−1, h must be in J·s.

choices.text: J/K
choices.why: J/K is the unit of Boltzmann's constant. Planck's constant is in J·s.

choices.text: m/s
choices.why: m/s is a speed, such as the speed of light. Planck's constant is in J·s.

explanation: h = 6.626 × 10^−34 J·s. Since E = hν and frequency is in s^−1, h must have units of energy times time.

prompt: In Planck's picture, why does a blackbody give off very little ultraviolet radiation?

choices.text: An ultraviolet quantum carries a lot of energy, and it is more probable to emit many lower-energy quanta than one very high-energy quantum
Ultraviolet light is absorbed by the walls of the oven
choices.why: The oven walls are not the reason. It is simply less probable to emit one large ultraviolet quantum than many smaller ones.

choices.text: Ultraviolet quanta carry less energy than visible quanta
choices.why: It is the other way round: E = hν, and ultraviolet light has a higher frequency, so each quantum carries more energy.

choices.text: Blackbodies are never hot enough to emit any ultraviolet
choices.why: Very hot objects do emit some ultraviolet. Planck's point is that high-energy quanta are less probable, so the intensity falls off.

explanation: At any temperature it is more probable for an object to lose energy by emitting many lower-energy quanta than a single very high-energy quantum, such as one of ultraviolet light. This gives the intensity curve a maximum instead of the ultraviolet catastrophe.

prompt: What are the packets of light energy, each of size hν, called?

choices.text: Photons
Electrons
choices.why: Electrons are particles of matter. The quanta of light energy are photons.

choices.text: Protons
choices.why: Protons are particles in the nucleus. The quanta of light energy are photons.

choices.text: Neutrons
choices.why: Neutrons are uncharged particles in the nucleus. The quanta of light energy are photons.

explanation: The energy carried by light is quantized in units of hν, and these packets of energy are called photons.

prompt: How did Planck himself first see his quantum assumption?

choices.text: As a technical fix that he hoped would eventually prove unnecessary
As proof that light is made of particles
choices.why: Planck did not draw that conclusion. He did not believe his own assumption at first, and saw it as a technical fix.

choices.text: As something Maxwell's laws had already predicted
choices.why: Nothing in Maxwell's laws suggested quantized energy, which is why the idea was so hard to accept.

choices.text: As an idea he took from Bohr's model of the atom
choices.why: Bohr's model came later, in 1913, and built on Planck's idea, not the other way round.

explanation: Planck did not believe his quantum assumption at first. He saw it as a technical fix that he hoped would prove unnecessary, even though more and more accurate experiments confirmed his blackbody curve.

prompt: How did physicists of the late 19th century view matter and electromagnetic radiation?

choices.text: As distinct and unrelated things
As two forms of the same thing
choices.why: Physicists then saw them as separate: matter as particles with mass, and radiation as massless with no fixed position.

choices.text: As both made of particles with mass
choices.why: Only matter was pictured as particles with mass. Radiation was seen as having no mass and no exact position in space.

choices.text: As both quantized in units of hν
choices.why: Quantization came only with Planck in 1900. Before that, matter and radiation were considered distinct and unrelated.

explanation: Matter was pictured as particles with mass whose position and motion could be described exactly, and electromagnetic radiation as massless with no fixed position. So matter and energy were considered distinct and unrelated.

prompt: In the late 19th century, what did Maxwell's equations describe?

choices.text: The properties of electromagnetic radiation
The motions of material objects, such as planets
choices.why: Those were calculated with Newton's laws of classical mechanics. Maxwell's equations described radiant energy.

choices.text: The quantized energies of atomic oscillators
choices.why: Nothing in Maxwell's laws suggested quantized energy; that was Planck's new idea. Maxwell's equations described electromagnetic radiation.

choices.text: The arrangement of electrons inside atoms
choices.why: Maxwell's equations of 1873 are about electromagnetic radiation, such as light and radio waves, not the structure of atoms.

explanation: In 1873 James Clerk Maxwell developed equations that describe the properties of radiant energy, that is, electromagnetic radiation. Newton's laws, by contrast, described the motions of material objects.

prompt: What does the measured intensity of blackbody radiation actually do at very short wavelengths?

choices.text: It drops toward zero
It rises without limit
choices.why: That was the classical Rayleigh-Jeans prediction, the ultraviolet catastrophe. Measurements show the intensity falling to zero.

choices.text: It levels off at a constant value
choices.why: The measured curve does not level off; after its peak it falls sharply toward zero at short wavelengths.

choices.text: It reaches its highest value
choices.why: The maximum lies at a middle wavelength that depends on temperature. At very short wavelengths the intensity falls toward zero.

explanation: The Rayleigh-Jeans theory predicted that the intensity should go to infinity at short wavelengths, but the measured intensity drops to zero there. This disagreement was the ultraviolet catastrophe.

prompt: An ion can have a charge of −1 or −2 electron charges, but never −1.33. What does this show about electrical charge?

choices.text: It is quantized
It is continuous
choices.why: A continuous quantity could take any value, including −1.33. Charge comes only in whole units, so it is quantized.

choices.text: It is always negative
choices.why: Ions can be positive or negative. The point is that charge comes only in whole-number units: it is quantized.

choices.text: It depends on the temperature
choices.why: The allowed values do not change with temperature. Charge comes in whole units, so it is quantized.

explanation: Quantized means only certain separate values are allowed. Charge comes in whole-number multiples of the electron charge, just as US money comes in whole pennies.

prompt: Why does the section call the notes of a piano quantized?

choices.text: It can produce only certain frequencies
It can produce any frequency at all
choices.why: That would be continuous. A piano has a fixed set of notes, such as C or F sharp, so its frequencies are quantized.

choices.text: Its keys are pressed one at a time
choices.why: How the keys are pressed is not the point. The instrument can produce only certain frequencies, so its frequencies are quantized.

choices.text: Each of its notes lasts a short time
choices.why: How long a note lasts does not matter. Quantized means only certain values are allowed, and a piano can produce only certain frequencies.

explanation: A piano or a trumpet can produce only certain notes, such as C or F sharp, not a continuous range of frequencies. So its frequencies are quantized, like energy in Planck's theory.

prompt: In Planck's model of blackbody radiation, what gives off and takes up the radiation?

choices.text: Oscillating charges (electrons) in the oven walls
Air molecules drifting inside the oven
choices.why: Planck modeled the oscillating charges in the walls, which radiate heat inwards and are themselves driven by the radiation.

choices.text: Nuclei breaking apart in the oven walls
choices.why: Nothing breaks apart. Planck modeled electrons oscillating in the walls, much as oscillating electrons in an antenna make radio waves.

choices.text: Electrons flying out of the walls into the oven
choices.why: The electrons stay in the walls and oscillate, like the electrons in an antenna. Their oscillations give off and take up the radiation.

explanation: Planck explained blackbody radiation as coming from oscillations of electrons, the oscillating charges in the oven walls, much as oscillating electrons in an antenna produce radio waves. These oscillators could gain or lose energy only in quanta of hν.

prompt: How well did Planck's radiation formula match the measured blackbody curves?

choices.text: Very well, at every temperature
Only at long wavelengths
choices.why: That describes the classical Rayleigh-Jeans law. Planck's formula agreed excellently with experiment at all temperatures.

choices.text: Only at very high temperatures
choices.why: Planck's formula fit the data at all temperatures, and more and more accurate experiments kept confirming it.

choices.text: Poorly; it still predicted infinite ultraviolet energy
choices.why: Planck's formula removed the ultraviolet catastrophe: it gives a curve with a maximum, matching experiment.

explanation: Planck's equation gave excellent agreement with experiment at all temperatures, and more and more accurate experiments confirmed it time and again. His blackbody curve was completely accepted as the correct one.

prompt: The Sun is an excellent approximation of a blackbody. About what is its effective temperature?

choices.text: About 5800 K
About 300 K
choices.why: That is about room temperature, where a body radiates mostly infrared and looks black. The Sun's effective temperature is about 5800 K.

choices.text: About 1000 K
choices.why: A body at about 1000 K glows only dull red. The Sun, at about 5800 K, gives off light that is close to white.

choices.text: About 1,000,000 K
choices.why: That is far too hot: such a body would peak at wavelengths much shorter than visible light. The Sun's effective temperature is about 5800 K.

explanation: The Sun's effective temperature is about 5777 K, and the blackbody curve for an object at 6000 K closely matches the spectrum of sunlight.

prompt: Who later pointed out that Planck had made contradictory assumptions on his route to the blackbody formula?

choices.text: Einstein
Rayleigh
choices.why: Rayleigh worked on the classical law that failed. It was Einstein who noticed the contradictions in Planck's route, though the result was correct.

choices.text: Maxwell
choices.why: Maxwell developed the equations of electromagnetic radiation in 1873. Einstein pointed out the contradictions in Planck's work.

choices.text: Jeans
choices.why: Jeans, with Rayleigh, developed the classical law that failed. Einstein pointed out the contradictions in Planck's route.

explanation: Planck's route to his formula was long, difficult and implausible, and Einstein later pointed out that he had even made contradictory assumptions at different stages. The result was correct anyway.

prompt: The section imagines a mass on a spring whose energy is quantized, like Planck's oscillators. How would it lose energy as friction slows it down?

choices.text: By jumping from one fixed energy to the next
By slowing smoothly through every energy in between
choices.why: That is the classical, continuous picture. A quantized oscillator jumps from one allowed energy to another.

choices.text: It could never lose any of its energy
choices.why: It can lose energy, but only in whole quanta, jumping from one fixed energy to the next.

choices.text: By losing all of its energy in one single jump
choices.why: It need not lose everything at once: it moves down from one allowed energy to the next, without passing through the energies in between.

explanation: If energy is quantized, a vibrating mass coming to rest would not slow down smoothly. It would jump from one fixed quantity of energy to another without passing through the intermediate energies.

prompt: At first, Planck's hypothesis explained only one set of data, blackbody radiation. According to the section, what would make quantization a law?

choices.text: Seeing quantization in many different phenomena
Planck explaining why energy is quantized
choices.why: A law comes from observation. The section says a theory explaining the law might be developed later.

choices.text: One more, very precise blackbody measurement
choices.why: More blackbody data would still be only one phenomenon. Quantization would become a law if it were seen in many different phenomena.

choices.text: Finding that Maxwell's laws predicted it
choices.why: Nothing in Maxwell's laws suggested quantized energy. Quantization would become a law by being observed in many different phenomena.

explanation: If quantization were observed for many different phenomena, it would become a law, and in time a theory might be developed to explain that law. Planck's hypothesis turned out to be the seed from which modern physics grew.

prompt: What did the agreement between Planck's theory and the experimental blackbody curves give strong evidence for?

choices.text: The energy of electron motion in matter is quantized
Classical physics fully explains blackbody radiation
choices.why: The opposite: classical physics failed. Planck's success depended on quantized energy.

choices.text: Atoms have a small, dense nucleus
choices.why: That came from other experiments. Planck's agreement was evidence that the energy of electron motion in matter is quantized.

choices.text: Light always travels at the same speed
choices.why: Blackbody curves say nothing about the speed of light. Planck's success was evidence that the energy of electron motion in matter is quantized.

explanation: Planck's formula fit the data only by assuming that the oscillating electrons gain or lose energy in quanta of hν. So its success was strong evidence that the energy of electron motion in matter is quantized.

prompt: Planck's formula gives the energy density of the radiation inside the oven. In what units is an energy density measured?

choices.text: J/m^3
W/m^2
choices.why: W/m^2 is a power per area. An energy density is an energy per volume, J/m^3.

choices.text: J·s
choices.why: J·s is the unit of Planck's constant. An energy density is an energy per volume, J/m^3.

choices.text: J/K
choices.why: J/K is the unit of Boltzmann's constant, k_B. An energy density is an energy per volume, J/m^3.

explanation: A density is an amount per volume, so an energy density is in joules per cubic meter, J/m^3. Exercise 1.2.1 asks you to check that Planck's ρ(λ, T) dλ comes out in J/m^3.

prompt: In Planck's picture, what changes as a blackbody gets hotter?

choices.text: Higher-frequency quanta become more likely
Each quantum of a given frequency gets larger
choices.why: The size of a quantum, hν, depends only on the frequency, not on the temperature. What changes is how likely higher-frequency quanta are.

choices.text: It emits only lower-frequency radiation
choices.why: It is the reverse: at low temperatures only low frequencies are emitted, and heating makes higher frequencies more likely.

choices.text: Its energy is no longer quantized at all
choices.why: Energy stays quantized at every temperature. Heating just makes higher-energy quanta more probable.

explanation: At low temperatures only low-frequency, low-energy quanta are emitted. As the temperature rises, emitting higher-frequency, higher-energy quanta becomes more probable, so the peak shifts to higher frequency (shorter wavelength).

prompt: The section suggests that what look like smooth inclined planes may really be closely spaced steps. Why would such steps seem smooth?

choices.text: The steps are so close they look continuous
They are so large that we only ever see one
choices.why: Large steps would be easy to notice. Tiny, closely spaced steps give the illusion of continuity.

choices.text: There are no steps; energy is truly continuous
choices.why: The analogy says the steps are really there. They are just so closely spaced that they give the illusion of continuity.

choices.text: The steps exist only inside hot ovens
choices.why: The analogy is general: steps that are close enough together look smooth wherever they are.

explanation: The section's analogy is that smooth inclined planes are really a series of closely spaced steps that only present the illusion of continuity. In the same way, quantized energies that are very close together can look continuous.

prompt: Why does a blackbody at a very high temperature look white?

choices.text: It emits all visible colors about equally
It emits light of one single white wavelength
choices.why: There is no single white wavelength. White light is a mix of all the visible colors in about equal amounts.

choices.text: It stops giving off any infrared radiation
choices.why: A hot body still emits infrared. It looks white because it emits all visible wavelengths about equally.

choices.text: It reflects the white light around it
choices.why: A blackbody absorbs light rather than reflecting it. Its white glow is its own emission, spread about evenly over the visible.

explanation: At high temperatures a blackbody emits all wavelengths of visible light with approximately equal intensities, so it looks white. At lower temperatures it emits mostly at longer wavelengths and looks red, orange or yellow.

prompt: In Planck's theory an oscillator's energy is E = nhν, where n is a whole number. Use h = 6.626 × 10^−34 J·s. What is the energy, in J, of an oscillator with frequency ν = 5.00 × 10^13 Hz and n = 3? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e-19.)
An oscillator can lose energy only in quanta of hν = 4.0 × 10^−20 J. If it loses a total of 1.2 × 10^−19 J, how many quanta has it given off?
explanation: Number of quanta = (1.2 × 10^−19 J)/(4.0 × 10^−20 J) = 3. Energy changes only in whole-number multiples of hν.

prompt: Use E = hν, so ν = E/h, with h = 6.626 × 10^−34 J·s. One quantum of radiation carries 3.313 × 10^−19 J. What is its frequency, in Hz? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e13.)
Use E = hν. How many times more energy does one quantum of ultraviolet radiation with ν = 1.5 × 10^15 Hz carry than one quantum of infrared radiation with ν = 3.0 × 10^14 Hz?
explanation: E is proportional to ν, so the ratio of the energies is the ratio of the frequencies: (1.5 × 10^15 Hz)/(3.0 × 10^14 Hz) = 5. Each ultraviolet quantum is a much bigger chunk of energy, which is why a blackbody emits few of them.
